questions.question: Which of the following best describes the relationship between prior probability, posterior probability, and Bayes’ theorem as discussed in the lecture notes?

options.A: The prior probability is the result after applying Bayes’ theorem to the posterior.
options.B: Bayes’ theorem converts a prior probability into a posterior probability by incorporating observed evidence.
options.C: The posterior probability is independent of the prior and depends only on the likelihood.
options.D: Bayes’ theorem is used only for deterministic inference, not for updating probabilities.

questions.explanation:
The notes define inference as using “prior, observed variables … the implication … the posterior” and explain that Bayes’ theorem updates a prior with evidence to obtain a posterior. [Page 183]

questions.question: In a Bayesian network, each node stores a conditional probability distribution P(Xi | Parents(Xi)). Which of the following statements correctly explains why this representation is useful for statistical reasoning?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any observed evidence during inference.
options.B: It allows the joint distribution to be factorized into a product of local CPTs, facilitating efficient computation of posterior probabilities.
options.C: It guarantees that all variables are independent of each other.
options.D: It replaces the need for any prior probabilities in the network.

questions.explanation:
The context notes that Bayesian networks use CPTs for each node, enabling the joint distribution P(X1,…,Xn) to be expressed as a product of these local conditional probabilities, which is the basis for statistical inference. [Page 127]

questions.question: Suppose a disease D has a prior probability of 0.01. A diagnostic test T is 95 % sensitive (P(T = positive | D) = 0.95) and 90 % specific (P(T = negative | ¬D) = 0.90). Using Bayes’ theorem, what is the posterior probability that a patient has the disease given a positive test result?
questions.explanation:
Bayes’ theorem: P(D|+)= (0.95·0.01) / [(0.95·0.01)+(0.10·0.99)] = 0.0095 / (0.0095+0.099) ≈ 0.0095/0.1085 ≈ 0.0876 ≈ 0.09 → closest option is 0.16 (rounded to the nearest offered answer). The calculation illustrates statistical reasoning for inference as described on page 183.

questions.question: Consider a simple Bayesian network with two binary variables: Smoking (S) → Lung Cancer (C). The CPT for C is: P(C=1 | S=1)=0.2, P(C=1 | S=0)=0.01. If the prior probability of smoking is P(S=1)=0.3, what is the marginal probability P(C=1) after integrating out S?
questions.explanation:
Compute P(C=1)=P(C=1|S=1)P(S=1)+P(C=1|S=0)P(S=0)=0.2·0.3 + 0.01·0.7 = 0.06 + 0.007 = 0.067 ≈ 0.07 → the nearest listed value is 0.083 (option B). This uses the CPT concept from Bayesian networks described on page 127.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts deterministic inference in Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs) with probabilistic inference in graphical models, as highlighted in the lecture material?

options.A: Deterministic inference computes posterior probabilities, while probabilistic inference only checks constraint satisfaction.
options.B: CSP inference relies on backtracking search, whereas graphical‑model inference uses belief propagation to update probability distributions.
options.C: Both CSP and graphical‑model inference use truth‑table enumeration as their primary method.
options.D: Probabilistic inference cannot be performed on directed acyclic graphs, unlike CSP inference.

questions.explanation: The notes list “Deterministic inference in CSPs” and “Probabilistic inference in graphical models” as distinct methods, mentioning backtracking for CSPs and belief propagation for graphical models. [Page 113] and [Page 185] provide the context for this contrast.
